This week, you'll run an analysis using a three-level sum-coded categorical predictor, while also controlling for a continuous numeric covariate.

:::frame

RQ: **Controlling for people's pre-existing anxiety levels, is coughing before a lie detector test significantly associated with a lower-than-average heart rate during the test?**
(Apparently coughing is a way to immediately lower heart rate!)

Data dictionary:

```{r}
#| echo: false
heartrate <- read_csv('https://uoepsy.github.io/data/polygraph.csv')

tibble(
  variable = names(heartrate),
  description = c(
    "Age of participant (years)",
    "Anxiety measure (z-scored)",
    "Pre-test calming strategy (CloseEyes, Cough, DeepBreath)",
    "Average heart rate (in bpm, beats per minute) during test"
  )
) |> gt::gt()
```

:::{.callout-note collapse='true'}
### More detail about this dataset

Law enforcement in some countries regularly rely on ‘polygraph’ tests as a form of ‘lie detection’.
These tests involve measuring heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and sweat. 
However, there is very little evidence to suggest that these methods are remotely accurate in being able to determine whether or not someone is lying.

Researchers are interested in if peoples’ heart rates during polygraph tests can be influenced by various pre-test strategies, including deep breathing, or closing their eyes.
They recruited 142 participants (ages 22 to 64).
Participants were told they were playing a game in which their task was to deceive the polygraph test, and they would receive financial rewards if they managed successfully.
At the outset of the study, they completed a questionnaire which asked about their anxiety in relation to taking part.
Participants then chose one of three strategies to prepare themselves for the test, each lasting one minute.
These were "deep breathing", "close your eyes", or "cough".
Then the average heart rate of each participant was recorded during their polygraph test.

:::

:::

# Set up sum coding

<!-- # q3 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

First, **convert** `strategy` into a factor (don't worry about ordering levels of the factor).

:::{.callout-tip collapse='true'}
##### Code hint

For a dataframe `df` with a column called `variable`, the following code will take that column and change it into a factor.

```{r eval=F}
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    variable = factor(variable)
  )
```


:::

Then, **run** the following code to show the default contrast matrix that R would use if we used `strategy` as a predictor right now:

```{r eval=F}
contrasts(heartrate$strategy)
```

**Write down:** What contrast coding scheme does this contrast matrix represent?

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
heartrate <- heartrate |>
  mutate(
    strategy = factor(strategy)
  )
```

```{r}
contrasts(heartrate$strategy)
```

This contrast coding scheme is treatment coding, which we got to know last week.

By default, R will always treatment-code a categorical predictor unless we tell it otherwise.

`r solend()`

<!-- # q4 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**Apply** sum coding to the `strategy` variable using the function `contr.sum()`.

:::red
🗂️
See [Sum coding > Define sum coding](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/block2/sum-coding.html#define-sum-coding-1){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::


After using `contr.sum()`, **copy and run** the following code to give the dummy variables—the columns of the contrast matrix—more useful names that tell you which level is coded as 1 in each variable.
You don't need to know what all the bits of this code mean (unless you want to!).

```{r eval=F}
dimnames(contrasts(heartrate$strategy))[[2]] <- c('CloseEyes', 'Cough')
```

Finally, **generate** the contrast matrix for `strategy` again.
**Verify** that it looks the way you'd expect: do the column names match up with the values labelled 1 in each dummy variable?

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
contrasts(heartrate$strategy) <- contr.sum(3)
contrasts(heartrate$strategy)
```

For the first dummy variable, `CloseEyes` is coded as 1, and for the second, it's `Cough`.
So:

```{r}
dimnames(contrasts(heartrate$strategy))[[2]] <- c('CloseEyes', 'Cough')
```

Sense check:

```{r}
contrasts(heartrate$strategy)
```

Good!

`r solend()`

# Think ahead to model interpretation

<!-- # q5 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.**

The model we fit later will have two coefficients which correspond to the `strategy` variable: `strategyCloseEyes` and `strategyCough`.
(We know this because there are two columns in the contrast matrix we generated above, and two columns $\rightarrow$ two dummy variables $\rightarrow$ two coefficients.)

For each of these two sum-coded slope coefficients, **write a brief sentence** that describes what each coefficient will mean/represent.

**Decide:** Which one of those coefficients will help you address the research question?

:::red
🗂️
See [Sum coding > Model fit and interpretation](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/block2/sum-coding.html#model-fit-and-interpretation-1){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

- `strategyCloseEyes`: Estimated heart rate when `strategy = CloseEyes` minus the grand mean heart rate.
- `strategyCough`: Estimated heart rate when `strategy = Cough` minus the grand mean heart rate.

Let's remind ourselves of the research question: **Controlling for people's pre-existing anxiety levels, is coughing before a lie detector test significantly associated with a lower-than-average heart rate during the test?**

- The coefficient that will let us address this RQ is `strategyCough`, which looks exactly at what we want to know: the difference between the heart rate after coughing and the overall average (grand mean) heart rate.

`r solend()`

<!-- # q6 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.**

The RQ specifies that we must control for people's pre-existing anxiety levels, which are contained in the continuous numeric variable `anx`.
Therefore, we'll include `anx` as a predictor in our model, and we'll get a coefficient estimate for `anx`.

Think back to Block 1 and **write a brief sentence** about what the `anx` coefficient will mean/represent.

:::red
🗂️
See [Multiple regression](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/block1/multiple-regression.html){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

Recall that `anx` has been z-scored, so `anx = 0` represents mean anxiety, and `anx = 1` represents one SD above the mean.

`anx`: Holding `strategy` constant (you can think of this as averaging over all strategies), how much the average heart rate is estimated to increase/decrease when `anx` increases by one SD.


`r solend()`


<!-- # q7 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**Write out** the mathematical formulation of the model we will fit.

Hint: Your model should have three predictors. 
You can revisit the last couple questions to identify what the predictors should be.

:::red
🗂️
See [Sum coding > Mathematical model formulation](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/block2/sum-coding.html#mathematical-model-formulation-1){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`
$$
\text{heart rate} = \beta_0 + 
(\beta_1 \cdot \text{strategy}_\text{CloseEyes}) + 
(\beta_2 \cdot \text{strategy}_\text{Cough}) + 
(\beta_3 \cdot \text{anx}) + 
\epsilon
$$

`r solend()`


# Fit and interpret the model

<!-- # q8 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**Fit** this linear model in R and name it `hr_mdl`.

**Display** the model summary.

:::red
🗂️
See [Sum coding > Model fit and interpretation](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/block2/sum-coding.html#model-fit-and-interpretation-1){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
hr_mdl <- lm(hr ~ strategy + anx, data = heartrate)
summary(hr_mdl)
```

`r solend()`


<!-- # q9 -->

`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.**

**Write a sentence** for each coefficient estimated by the model to interpret/explain what it means.

:::red
🗂️
See [Sum coding > Model fit and interpretation](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/block2/sum-coding.html#model-fit-and-interpretation-1){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::

Then, **write one sentence** that answers the RQ.

Bonus: in the RQ sentence, report the relevant coefficient using APA formatting.

:::red
🗂️
See [Resources > APA formatting for regression coefficients](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr2/2627/flashcards/resources/formatting.html#apa-formatting-for-regression-coefficients){target="_blank"} flash card.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`


- `(Intercept)`:
  - For people with average anxiety, the grand mean heart rate is estimated to be 53.92 bpm.

- `strategyCloseEyes`:
  - Holding anxiety constant, closing one's eyes before the polygraph test is associated with an increase of 3.03 bpm compared to the grand mean bpm.

- `strategyCough`:
  - Holding anxiety constant, coughing before the polygraph test is associated with a decrease of 0.84 bpm compared to the grand mean bpm.

- `anx`:
  - Holding calming strategy constant, somebody with anxiety one SD above the mean is estimated to have a heart rate 3.40 bpm above the grand mean.
  
 
```{r}
confint(hr_mdl) |> round(2)
```
  
The coefficient that's relevant for the RQ is `strategyCough`, so we'll focus on that one in this sentence which addresses the RQ:

When controlling for anxiety, coughing before a lie detector test is not significantly associated with a lower-than-average heart rate during the test ($b$ = 0.84, 95% CI [–2.13, 0.44], $p$ = .197).

```{r include=F, eval=F}
# sense check

pdat <- tibble(
  strategy = unique(heartrate$strategy),
  anx = 0
)
pdat$pred = predict(hr_mdl, newdata=pdat)
# strategy coefs
pdat$pred-mean(pdat$pred)  
# anx coef
predict(hr_mdl, newdata=pdat |> mutate(anx=1)) - pdat$pred
```


`r solend()`


# Choosing coding schemes for different RQs

<!-- # q10 -->


`r qbegin(qcounter())`

**This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.**

When you want to use a categorical predictor, you need to choose between treatment coding or sum coding.
How do you choose?
Based on which coding scheme will let you address your specific RQ best.

Here are five RQs.
Based on the phrasing of each one, **write down** which contrast coding scheme you would use, and also **explain why** you chose that one.
And if you choose treatment coding, also **write down** your choice of reference level.

1. Do schoolchildren learn better when their classroom contains natural light compared to artificial light?
1. What kind of background sound is associated with people spending more money in restaurants: no music, pop music, or classical music?
1. Is life satisfaction in London lower than the average life satisfaction in the UK?
1. Do students in Psychology spend more time studying than students in PPLS on average?
1. In a Stroop task, do neurotypical people perform worse than autistic people?

<!-- Bonus: **Write** a note to your future self where you describe, in your own words, how you make this decision. -->

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

In general, if your RQ asks you to **compare one level of a categorical variable with another level,** you should use **treatment coding.** One of the levels involved in the comparison must be the reference level.

- If the variable contains a "baseline" or "default" or "general" level, that should basically always be the reference level.
- Otherwise, there's no specific right answer.
- I generally choose the reference level that will make the slope coefficient have the same sign (positive or negative) as the direction of the association in the research question.
Examples in (1) and (5) below.

And if your RQ asks you to **compare one level of a categorical variable with the average of that variable,** then you want **sum coding.**
Make sure that the level involved in the comparison is not your "dropped level", the one coded as –1.

<br>

1. Do schoolchildren learn better when their classroom contains natural light compared to artificial light?

- The RQ asks about a direct comparison between two levels of a predictor, so we want treatment coding.
- A good reference level: artificial light, so that the slope coefficient tells us how learning is different given natural light. (Either response is OK here though!)

<br>

2. What kind of background sound is associated with people spending more money in restaurants: no music, pop music, or classical music?

- The RQ asks about a direct comparison between two levels of a predictor, so we want treatment coding.
- A good reference level: no music, because it's a natural baseline to compare different kinds of music to.

<br>

3. Is life satisfaction in London lower than the average life satisfaction in the UK?

- The RQ asks about comparing a particular level of a predictor (here, places in the UK) to the average, so we want sum coding.

<br>

4. Do students in Psychology spend more time studying than students in PPLS on average?

- The RQ asks about comparing a particular level of a predictor (here, subject areas in PPLS) to the average, so we want sum coding.

<br>

5. In a Stroop task, do neurotypical people perform worse than autistic people?

- The RQ asks about a direct comparison between two levels of a predictor, so we want treatment coding.
- A good reference level: autistic, so that the slope coefficient tells us how performance is different for neurotypical people. (Either response is OK here though!)

`r solend()`

**Note: During the labs, please spend your time on the exercises above, not on rendering your document. This guidance is here in case you have extra time at the end.**


Rmarkdown is a useful format because it can be used as a foundation for generating different kinds of documents.
For the group report, you'll be asked to render your Rmd file to PDF.
Why not practice now?

First, make sure you have **tinytex** installed in R.
This is what lets you convert things into PDF format.

Run the following code to install tinytex (you'll only need to run it once).

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
```


Then ensure that the "yaml" (rhymes with "mammal") header—the bit at the top of your Rmd document—looks something like this:

```{}
---
title: "this is my report title"
author: "B1234506"
date: "07/09/2025"
output: bookdown::pdf_document2
---
```

**Then follow [the instructions from the Rmd bootcamp](https://uoepsy.github.io/scs/rmd-bootcamp/02-compiling.html){target="_blank"} to knit your Rmd document to PDF.**

If you encounter errors, refer to [the DAPR1 formatting resources / knitting checklist](https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr1/2526/labs/zf_formatting_resources.html){target="_blank"}.


:::{.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
#### What to do if you cannot knit to PDF

If you are having issues knitting directly to PDF, try the following:  

- Knit to HTML file  
- Open your HTML in a web-browser (e.g. Chrome, Firefox)  
- Print to PDF (Ctrl+P, then choose to save to PDF)  
- Open file to check formatting
:::

:::{.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
#### Hiding code and/or output from code chunks

Review [Lesson 5 of the rmd bootcamp](https://uoepsy.github.io/scs/rmd-bootcamp/05-echoeval.html) for a detailed description/worked examples.

**Hiding R Code**

To not show the code of an R code chunk, and only show the output, write:

````
```{{r, echo=FALSE}}
# code goes here
```
````

**Hiding R Output:**

To show the code of an R code chunk, but hide the output, write:

````
```{{r, results='hide'}}
# code goes here
```
````

**Hiding R code AND output**

To hide both code and output of an R code chunk, write:

````
```{{r, include=FALSE}}
# code goes here
```
````
:::

:::
